name: Conduit Lamprey
description:
Lake Michigan has always had sea lampreys. The Conduit Lamprey is what happens when lamprey larvae spend two centuries filtering through GLMZ's intake and drainage infrastructure instead of open water. They are smaller than their lake ancestors — the largest reach sixty centimeters — and their bodies have become more eel-like, with reduced dorsal fin structure that allows full-body compression. The iconic toothed sucker mouth persists entirely, perhaps more pronounced, ringed with micro-serrated keratin teeth evolved finer for gripping biofilm-coated concrete and PVC pipe walls rather than fish scales. They are pale yellow-white with a faintly iridescent slick to their skin from the biofilm communities they carry.

Conduit Lampreys are not primarily parasitic in the classical sense — their drainage-adapted diet is mostly biofilm scraping, fungal mat consumption, and occasional filter-feeding on organic particulate in slow-flow sections. However, they retain the capacity for parasitic attachment and will opportunistically feed on any warm animal immobilized in water, including humans who fall into flooded tunnels. They navigate entirely by electroreception and lateral line pressure sensing. They are remarkable climbers of wet vertical surfaces — their sucker mouth allows them to ascend wet concrete walls, and populations have been found well above the waterline in drainage shafts, clinging to walls in clusters.

The wall-clustering behavior is what earns them their most common slang name. Infrastructure inspectors entering drainage shafts sometimes play their lights up the walls and find dozens of pale bodies pressed flat in overlapping rings, motionless until disturbed. This image has entered GLMZ's informal visual culture — a particular style of street mosaic in flooded Shelf corridors depicting ring-mouthed forms climbing walls is called 'lamprey tile' and signals that the building's basement has water problems. They are generally considered disgusting rather than dangerous, but the combination of sucker-mouth and opportunistic parasitism means that tunnel workers maintain a healthy respect.
diet: Biofilm, fungal mats, organic particulate, opportunistic parasitism on immobilized animals
notable_traits: Wall-climbing sucker mouth with micro-serrated keratin teeth
Clustering behavior on wet vertical surfaces
Reduced dorsal fin for pipe compression
encounters: Most unsettling encounters occur when inspectors enter drainage shafts and illuminate wall clusters. Also found in flooded basements of older Shelf buildings, attached to walls above the waterline. Occasionally discovered in water storage tanks of poorly maintained Tier 1 buildings.
known_uses: The biofilm communities on their skin have been of minor research interest for industrial bioremediation applications. Otherwise considered a nuisance indicator species — their presence signals biofilm accumulation and potential flow restriction in drainage systems.
story_hooks: A Tier 3 residential building's water pressure has been dropping. The building manager insists it's infrastructure age. A Conduit Lamprey is found in a resident's tap filter — something is wrong much further up the system than the building manager wants to admit.

Someone is collecting live Conduit Lampreys in bulk from a specific drainage network section — the only reason anyone can figure out is that the biofilm those particular lampreys carry is chemically unusual, consistent with a spill or dump that was never reported.
